---
title: "Preparing Your Data"
subtitle: "From raw climate datasets to SPI/SPEI-ready inputs"
---

## Overview

Global climate datasets come from various providers, each with their own conventions for file formats, dimension ordering, variable naming, and temporal structure. Before calculating SPI or SPEI, your data must meet the [input contract](../get-started/data-model.qmd) expected by this package.

This tutorial provides practical guidance on preparing common datasets for SPI/SPEI calculation.

---

## What Makes Data "Ready"?

The package expects:

| Requirement | Expected | Common issues |
|-------------|----------|---------------|
| **Format** | NetCDF (`.nc`) | GeoTIFF time series, GRIB |
| **Dimensions** | `(time, lat, lon)` | Wrong order, missing time |
| **Coordinates** | Named `time`, `lat`, `lon` | `latitude`, `longitude`, `x`, `y` |
| **Time** | datetime64 with regular intervals | Integer indices, irregular spacing |
| **Units** | mm/month (precipitation) | mm/day, kg/m²/s |
| **Values** | Non-negative, NaN for missing | Fill values like -9999, negative values |

---

## Common Data Sources

| Dataset | Provider | Resolution | Format | Ready for SPI? |
|---------|----------|------------|--------|----------------|
| [CHIRPS](https://www.chc.ucsb.edu/data/chirps) | CHC/UCSB | 0.05° daily/monthly, **latitude-banded, not global** | NetCDF, GeoTIFF | Monthly NetCDF: Yes |
| [TerraClimate](https://www.climatologylab.org/terraclimate.html) | Climatology Lab | ~4km monthly | NetCDF | Yes (with minor fixes) |
| [ERA5-Land](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/) | ECMWF/Copernicus | 0.1° hourly, daily, monthly | NetCDF, GRIB | Requires aggregation |
| [GPM IMERG](https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/imerg) | NASA | 0.1° half-hourly, daily, monthly | NetCDF (HDF5) | Requires aggregation |

---

## Typical Preparation Steps

### 1. Convert to NetCDF (if needed)

Many datasets ship as one GeoTIFF per timestep. Stacking them into a NetCDF with
a real time axis is mechanical, and there is one detail that silently ruins the
result if you miss it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The half-pixel shift

A GeoTIFF's geotransform describes the **outer corner** of the top-left pixel.
A NetCDF coordinate variable describes the **centre** of each cell.

Copy the geotransform origin straight into a coordinate array and the entire
grid sits half a pixel off. On a 4 km grid that is 2 km. Nothing raises, no
check fails, and the data simply does not line up with anything else you
compare it against.

```python
res_x, res_y = transform.a, transform.e        # res_y is negative
lon = transform.c + np.arange(nx) * res_x + res_x / 2     # + half a pixel
lat = transform.f + np.arange(ny) * res_y + res_y / 2     # + half a pixel
```

Verified on a deliberately awkward grid: an origin at 100.0 E with 0.05 degree
cells must give a first cell centre of **100.025**, not 100.0.
:::

The second trap is consistency. If one raster in the folder sits on a different
grid, a naive loop writes it into the stack anyway and you get a time series
that jumps in space.

Use `scripts/tiff2nc.py`, which handles both:

```python
from scripts.tiff2nc import tiffs_to_netcdf

tiffs_to_netcdf(
    "geotiff/",
    "chirps_monthly_1981_2025.nc",
    var_name="precip",
    date_pattern=r"(\d{8})",      # one capture group
    date_format="%Y%m%d",
    units="mm",
    standard_name="precipitation_amount",
    lat_order="descending",        # keep the GeoTIFF's native row order
)
```

```
files     : 540  1981-01 .. 2025-12
grid      : 2400 x 7200  res 0.050000 x 0.050000  crs EPSG:4326
lon       : -179.975000 .. 179.975000  (cell centres)
lat       : 59.975000 .. -59.975000  (descending)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the script does beyond the half-pixel fix

- **Grid validation.** Every file's size and geotransform is compared against
  the first. A mismatch raises rather than being written into the stack.
- **Per-file nodata.** The nodata value is read from each raster and converted,
  instead of assuming a single sentinel across the folder.
- **Explicit date parsing.** The timestamp is pulled with a regex you supply and
  parsed with `strptime`. A filename that does not match raises. Files are then
  sorted by the parsed date, not by string order, and duplicate timestamps are
  rejected.
- **Latitude order is a choice you make.** `descending` copies rows as they are;
  `ascending` flips both the coordinate and the data together. Neither is more
  correct, but a mismatch between the two is a silent north-south flip, so the
  script never leaves it implicit.
- **CF metadata.** `Conventions`, a `crs` grid-mapping variable carrying the
  source WKT and EPSG code, coordinate `standard_name` / `units` / `axis`, and
  computed `geospatial_*` bounds as global attributes, which is where ACDD puts
  them.
- **Chunking** set for time-series access rather than left to the default.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: GDAL and CDO

```bash
# One GeoTIFF -> NetCDF, then concatenate along time
gdal_translate -of netCDF -co "FORMAT=NC4" input.tif output.nc
cdo -z zip_5 mergetime *.nc stacked.nc
```

Faster for a one-off, and `gdal_translate` gets the cell centres right. What you
give up is the time axis: GDAL writes no meaningful `time` coordinate from a
filename, so you still have to set units, calendar and values yourself. For a
handful of files that is fine; for a 540-file stack the Python route is less
work overall.
:::

---

### 2. Rename Coordinates

Renaming is the easy half. The half that matters is that a file calling its axis
`y` almost always also lacks `standard_name`, `units` and `axis`, and those are
what tell any other tool which way is north.

```python
import xarray as xr
from scripts.nc_fixups import standardise_names

ds = standardise_names(xr.open_dataset("input.nc"))
```

That maps the usual aliases (`latitude`/`longitude`, `x`/`y`, `nav_lat`, `t`,
`TIME`, ...) to `time`, `lat`, `lon`, then fills in the CF attributes **without
overwriting** anything the file already states. It also normalises longitude
from 0..360 to -180..180 and re-sorts, because the two conventions slice
differently and mixing them is a common source of empty selections.

To rename the data variable too:

```python
ds = standardise_names(ds, var_renames={"precipitation": "precip"})
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: NCO

```bash
ncrename -d latitude,lat -d longitude,lon -v latitude,lat -v longitude,lon in.nc out.nc
ncatted -a units,lat,o,c,"degrees_north" -a axis,lat,o,c,"Y" out.nc
```

`ncrename` needs both the dimension (`-d`) and the variable (`-v`); doing only
one leaves the file inconsistent. Note you then have to add the CF attributes by
hand with `ncatted`, which is the part people skip.
:::

---

### 3. Reorder Dimensions

The package expects `(time, lat, lon)`, and will transpose internally if it gets
something else. Doing it yourself is still worth it for anything you intend to
read more than once.

```python
from scripts.nc_fixups import order_dims

ds = order_dims(ds)                 # every 3-D variable -> (time, lat, lon)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## A transpose is not free once it reaches disk

`transpose` reorders the logical view immediately, but the bytes on disk keep
their original chunking. Reading a transposed view can therefore be far slower
than reading the original, because every logical row now spans many physical
chunks.

If you transpose, **write the result out**. Do not leave it lazy and read from
it repeatedly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: NCO and CDO

```bash
ncpdq -a time,lat,lon input.nc output.nc      # NCO, rewrites the file
cdo -z zip_5 copy input.nc output.nc          # CDO, also rechunks
```

`ncpdq -a` is the right tool here and is usually faster than the Python route
for a large file, because it streams.
:::

---

### 4. Convert Units

```python
from scripts.nc_fixups import convert_precip_units

ds = convert_precip_units(ds, "precip", source_units="kg m-2 s-1")
```

Handles rates per second, per hour and per day, plus metres to millimetres, and
updates the `units` attribute and `history` so the file records what happened.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Never use an average month length

Rate-to-total conversions must multiply by the **actual** length of each month.

| Month | Days | Error from a fixed 30.44 |
|:---|---:|---:|
| February, common year | 28 | **+8.71%** |
| February, leap year | 29 | +4.97% |
| April | 30 | +1.47% |
| July | 31 | −1.81% |

That is a 10.5 percentage-point systematic swing, and it is not noise: it is
locked to the calendar, so it lands directly on the seasonal cycle a drought
index exists to measure.

```python
days = ds.time.dt.days_in_month     # correct, and leap-year aware
```

Verified: converting 1 mm/day for February 2020 gives **29.0 mm**, not 30.44.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Check the units, do not assume them

`convert_precip_units` raises if the variable has no `units` attribute and you
did not supply one. That is deliberate. The same variable name ships in
different units depending on the product and the access route, and a silent
wrong guess here scales the entire dataset.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: CDO

```bash
cdo -z zip_5 -setattribute,precip@units=mm -mulc,86400 in.nc out.nc   # mm/s -> mm/day
cdo -z zip_5 monsum in.nc monthly.nc                                  # daily -> monthly total
```

`cdo monsum` sums each month correctly, including leap years, so for the
daily-to-monthly step it is both simpler and safer than hand arithmetic. The
`-mulc` route, though, is a fixed multiplier and cannot know the month length:
use it only for genuinely constant conversions such as metres to millimetres.
:::

---

### 5. Replace Zeros (only if you must)

Some fitting routines cannot take a zero, because the Gamma distribution is
undefined there. The usual workaround is to substitute a small positive value.

```python
from scripts.nc_fixups import replace_zeros

ds = replace_zeros(ds, "precip", value=0.001)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## You probably do not need this with `precip-index`

This package fits a **mixed distribution**: it counts the zeros, carries their
probability separately as `prob_zero`, and fits the continuous part to the
non-zero values. That is the statistically correct treatment of a variable with
an atom at zero.

Substituting 0.001 throws that away. It moves mass from the atom into the
continuous part and biases the fitted parameters, which matters most in exactly
the dry climates where zeros are common and where a drought index is most used.

Reach for this only when handing data to a tool that demands strictly positive
input.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Get the `where` the right way round, and keep NaN as NaN

`da.where(cond, other)` keeps values where `cond` is **True**. So the condition
must describe what you want to keep, which reads backwards to most people:

```python
da.where(da != 0, 0.001)     # correct: keeps non-zeros, replaces zeros
da.where(da == 0, 0.001)     # wrong: keeps ONLY the zeros, replaces everything else
```

NaN survives the correct form, because `NaN != 0` evaluates True. Demonstrated
on `[0.0, 1.5, NaN, 0.0, 3.2]`:

| Expression | Result |
|:---|:---|
| `da.where(da != 0, 0.001)` | `[0.001, 1.5, nan, 0.001, 3.2]` |
| `xr.where(da == 0, 0.001, da)` | `[0.001, 1.5, nan, 0.001, 3.2]` |
| `da.where(da == 0, 0.001)` | `[0.0, 0.001, 0.001, 0.0, 0.001]` |

The first two are equivalent and both preserve the missing value. The third
destroys the data.
:::

---

### 6. Handle Missing Values

```python
from scripts.nc_fixups import clean_missing

ds = clean_missing(ds, "precip")
```

```
precip: 21,048,332 of 34,040,217 missing (61.8%)
  never observed : 24,792,188 cells
  gaps in time   : 1,204 cells
```

Order matters, and the function fixes it: the value the file **declares**
first, then a list of common sentinels, then physical bounds. Applying a
`>= 0` filter before the sentinels leaves a `-9999` in place if you later only
test for exact matches; applying it afterwards costs nothing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why the split between "never observed" and "gaps in time" matters

A cell that is missing for the whole record is ocean, or outside the product's
footprint. It costs nothing: the index skips it.

A cell missing a scattered handful of months is different. It still gets fitted,
but on a shorter sample than its neighbours, and the fit silently becomes less
reliable. `precip-index` requires `MIN_VALUES_FOR_FIT` (20) values per calendar
month, so a cell with 11 or more missing years drops out entirely, while one
with 9 missing years is fitted on 21 values and looks identical in the output to
a cell fitted on 30.

The second number in that report is the one to watch, and it is the one a plain
"NaN count" hides completely.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: NCO

```bash
# Declare a fill value and convert a sentinel to it
ncatted -a _FillValue,precip,o,f,-9999.0 in.nc
ncap2 -s 'where(precip < 0) precip = precip@_FillValue;' in.nc out.nc
```

`ncap2` is the right tool for conditional rewrites on a file too large to open
in memory. The syntax is unforgiving; test on a subset first.
:::

---

### 7. Subset to Region of Interest

Processing global data is slow. Subset first if you only need a region.

#### By bounding box

```python
# slice() follows the STORED order of the axis, not numerical order. Get it
# backwards and you silently get zero rows, not an error. TerraClimate and
# most gridded products store latitude north-to-south.
south, north = -10, 0
if float(ds.lat[0]) > float(ds.lat[-1]):      # descending, north first
    ds_region = ds.sel(lat=slice(north, south), lon=slice(110, 120))
else:                                          # ascending, south first
    ds_region = ds.sel(lat=slice(south, north), lon=slice(110, 120))

assert ds_region.sizes['lat'] > 0, "empty selection: latitude order is reversed"
```

#### By shapefile

A one-line `rio.clip` works, and it will quietly cost you the edge of your
domain. Use `scripts/nc_clip.py`, which keeps every cell the polygon touches,
streams the time axis so a global file fits in memory, and writes CF-compliant
output:

```python
from scripts.nc_clip import clip_netcdf

clip_netcdf(
    "wld_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc",
    "WB_GAD_ADM0_AGO.shp",
    "ago_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc",
    all_touched=True,     # keep the boundary ring
    crop=True,            # shrink to the mask extent
    time_batch=24,        # time steps held in memory at once
)
```

```
shapefile : WB_GAD_ADM0_AGO.shp  (1 features, EPSG:4326)
input     : ppt float32 (816, 332, 303)
mask      : 60,725 cells (+1,015, 1.7% from all_touched)
output    : (816, 330, 301)  cropped
wrote     : ago_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc  (66.2 MB)
```

Or from the command line:

```bash
python scripts/nc_clip.py input.nc boundary.shp output.nc
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Keep the pixels the polygon touches

The default rasterisation rule keeps a cell only if its **centre** falls inside
the polygon. Every cell the boundary merely crosses is discarded, so you lose a
ring one cell wide around the whole domain.

Measured against the World Bank ADM0 boundaries on the TerraClimate grid:

| Area | Centre-only | `all_touched` | Gained | Perimeter/area |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DR Congo | 109,413 | 110,688 | **+1.2%** | 0.54 |
| Angola | 59,710 | 60,726 | **+1.7%** | 0.77 |
| Bali | 266 | 331 | **+24.4%** | 13.30 |

The loss scales with the perimeter-to-area ratio, not with size. For a large
compact country it is a rounding error. For an island, an archipelago or any
long thin basin it is not: a quarter of Bali disappears.

In every case 99-100% of the recovered cells sit directly against the retained
mask, which is to say they are exactly the coast and the border. That is usually
where the population is, and it is where a drought index gets used.

Do not take the table on trust for your own area. Measure it:

```bash
python scripts/measure_all_touched.py my_boundary.shp --res terraclimate
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What "CF-compliant output" means here

`clip_netcdf` writes `Conventions = "CF-1.8"` and, on the way, repairs what a
naive clip usually drops:

- coordinate variables get `standard_name`, `units` and `axis`
- a `crs` grid-mapping variable is written, and the data variable references it
  through `grid_mapping`
- `geospatial_lat_min` / `_max` / `_resolution` and the longitude equivalents
  describe the **clipped** extent, not the original
- the clip is appended to `history`, with the shapefile name and the rules used
- any `scale_factor`, `add_offset` or `missing_value` inherited from packed
  source data is dropped, because the output is real numbers

It also refuses rather than guesses: no CRS on the shapefile, no overlap with
the grid, or a polygon too small to select a single cell each raise instead of
silently producing an empty file.
:::

### 8. Ensure Regular Time Intervals

SPI/SPEI requires regular time spacing:

```python
import pandas as pd

# Check time spacing
times = pd.to_datetime(ds.time.values)
diffs = times.diff()[1:]
print(f"Time intervals: {diffs.unique()}")

# Resample to regular monthly if irregular.
# Precipitation accumulates, so it sums. Temperature averages.
precip_monthly = ds['precip'].resample(time='MS').sum()
temp_monthly = ds['temp'].resample(time='MS').mean()
```

---

## Validation Checklist

Before running SPI/SPEI, verify your prepared data:

```python
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset('prepared_data.nc')
precip = ds['precip']

# 1. Dimensions
print(f"Dimensions: {precip.dims}")
assert set(precip.dims) == {'time', 'lat', 'lon'}, "Missing dimensions"

# 2. Coordinate names
assert 'time' in ds.coords, "Missing time coordinate"
assert 'lat' in ds.coords, "Missing lat coordinate"
assert 'lon' in ds.coords, "Missing lon coordinate"

# 3. Time range (need ≥30 years)
years = precip.time.dt.year
n_years = int(years.max()) - int(years.min()) + 1   # inclusive
print(f"Period: {int(years.min())}-{int(years.max())} ({n_years} years)")

# 4. Values
print(f"Value range: [{precip.min().values:.2f}, {precip.max().values:.2f}]")
assert precip.min() >= 0, "Negative precipitation values found"

# 5. Missing data
missing_pct = float(precip.isnull().mean() * 100)
print(f"Missing: {missing_pct:.1f}%")

# 6. Units check (typical monthly precip: 0-500 mm/month)
mean_val = float(precip.mean())
print(f"Mean: {mean_val:.1f} mm/month")
if mean_val < 10:
    print("⚠️  Mean seems low — check if units are mm/day instead of mm/month")
if mean_val > 500:
    print("⚠️  Mean seems high — check units")

print("✓ Data appears ready for SPI/SPEI calculation")
```

### CF compliance

The checks above say the data is usable. These say the file describes itself, so
that the next person, or you in a year, does not have to guess.

```python
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset('prepared_data.nc', decode_cf=False)
var = ds['precip']
problems = []

# Conventions
if not str(ds.attrs.get('Conventions', '')).startswith('CF-'):
    problems.append("no Conventions attribute (expected e.g. 'CF-1.8')")

# Coordinate variables
for name, want_axis, want_units in (('lat', 'Y', 'degrees_north'),
                                    ('lon', 'X', 'degrees_east')):
    if name not in ds.coords:
        problems.append(f"missing coordinate {name}")
        continue
    a = ds[name].attrs
    if a.get('units') != want_units:
        problems.append(f"{name}.units is {a.get('units')!r}, expected {want_units!r}")
    if a.get('axis') != want_axis:
        problems.append(f"{name}.axis is {a.get('axis')!r}, expected {want_axis!r}")
    if 'standard_name' not in a:
        problems.append(f"{name} has no standard_name")

# Time needs units and a calendar to be unambiguous
t = ds['time'].attrs
if 'units' not in t:
    problems.append("time has no units (e.g. 'days since 1900-01-01')")
if 'calendar' not in t:
    problems.append("time has no calendar (defaults to 'standard', say so explicitly)")

# Grid mapping
gm = var.attrs.get('grid_mapping')
if gm is None:
    problems.append("variable has no grid_mapping attribute")
elif gm not in ds.variables:
    problems.append(f"grid_mapping points at {gm!r}, which does not exist")

# The variable itself
if 'units' not in var.attrs:
    problems.append("variable has no units")
for leftover in ('scale_factor', 'add_offset', '_Unsigned'):
    if leftover in var.attrs:
        problems.append(f"variable still carries {leftover}: unpack before use")

if problems:
    print("CF issues:")
    for p in problems:
        print(f"  - {p}")
else:
    print("✓ CF metadata complete")
```

Note `decode_cf=False`. With decoding on, xarray moves `scale_factor`,
`add_offset` and `_FillValue` out of `.attrs` and into `.encoding`, so a check
written against `.attrs` will report a packed file as clean.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Checking against the real standard

The checks above cover what matters for this package. For a full audit, the
[CF Conventions compliance checker](https://compliance.checker.ioos.us/) tests a
file against the published standard, including the controlled vocabulary of
`standard_name` values, which is longer than anyone remembers.
:::

---

## Dataset-Specific Guides

Each dataset has unique characteristics. See the detailed preparation guides:

::: {.grid-container}
::: {.feature-card}
### CHIRPS

Monthly precipitation at ~5 km, 1981-present, 60S-60N. NetCDF or GeoTIFF,
and the GeoTIFF trap that comes with it.

[CHIRPS Guide](00a-chirps.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
:::

::: {.feature-card}
### TerraClimate

Monthly precipitation and PET at ~4 km, 1950-present. Download, unpack the
packed integers, and merge into one series.

[TerraClimate Guide](00b-terraclimate.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
:::
:::

Guides for ERA5-Land and GPM IMERG are not written yet. The general steps above
apply to both; the dataset-specific traps are what the guides add.

---

## Quick Reference: Dataset Fixes

| Dataset | Key preparation steps |
|---------|----------------------|
| **CHIRPS monthly NetCDF** | Ready to use |
| **CHIRPS GeoTIFF series** | Combine into single NetCDF with time dimension |
| **TerraClimate** | Ready to use (variable `ppt` auto-detected) |
| **ERA5-Land** | Check the units attribute before converting. Do not assume: the same variable name is distributed in different units by different products and access routes |
| **IMERG monthly** | Ready to use (variable `precipitation` auto-detected) |
| **IMERG half-hourly/daily** | Aggregate to monthly; convert mm/hr → mm/month |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use monthly products when available
ERA5-Land and IMERG both offer pre-aggregated monthly products. These are much easier to work with — no temporal aggregation needed, just unit conversion (if any).
:::
